sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Two installation methods, set by the bar type. Solid bar soil nails, the most common, go in typically 4- to 8-in. diameter holes drilled and grouted in two steps: holes drilled at a shallow angle (usually 15 degrees from horizontal), cased or open, then tendons inserted and grouted. Hollow bar soil nails (HBSNs) are drilled and grouted in one operation, grout pumped through the bar and out of a sacrificial bit; faster in suitable ground and useful where open holes would collapse, but with limited corrosion protection options and QA and testing standards not fully established (Chapter 10).
sections.body: 3.1 Introduction (p. 33). The chapter presents materials and methods for soil nail wall construction. Standard installation techniques divide into two methods dictated by the type of bar. Solid bar soil nails are placed in typically 4- to 8-in. diameter drill holes drilled and grouted in a two-step operation: first the holes are drilled at a shallow angle (usually 15 degrees from horizontal) using cased or open-hole techniques; then the tendons are inserted and grouted. They are the most commonly used soil nails and are readily available in many tendon sizes, thread types and steel grades, with a variety of corrosion protection schemes. Hollow bar soil nails (HBSNs) are hollow, threaded steel tendons drilled and grouted in a single operation: grout is injected through the tendon as drilling proceeds, exits through ports in a sacrificial drill bit, flushes cuttings out of the hole, and fills the annulus between tendon and hole. Rotary and sometimes rotary-percussion drilling is used. HBSNs generally allow faster installation than solid bars in appropriate ground and are particularly advantageous where open holes would collapse and need temporary casing until grouting. Their corrosion protection schemes are limited, and standards for quality assurance and testing are not fully established (Chapter 10).
key_points: Solid bar nails: typically 4- to 8-in. holes, drilled then grouted (two steps); most common
Holes drilled at a shallow angle, usually 15 degrees from horizontal, cased or open
HBSNs: drilled and grouted in one operation through a sacrificial bit
HBSNs faster in suitable ground; useful where open holes would collapse
HBSNs: limited corrosion protection options; QA and testing standards not fully established (Chapter 10)

sections.title: Tendons
sections.summary: Tendons are threaded (continuous thread bars or cut threads, with the reduced area considered), at least 6 in. of thread at the face. Generally Grade 60 or 75 per ASTM A615; Grade 95 acceptable if ductility is comparable to lower grades; Grade 150 per ASTM A722, more typical of ground anchors. Common sizes Nos. 8-11; Nos. 6-7 often avoided (bending, close spacing), No. 14 and larger may be inefficient. Maximum manufactured length 60 ft (Nos. 6-14); couplers must develop the nominal tensile resistance. Hollow bars: yield 60 to 90 ksi, about 1 to 3 in. OD, 0.3 to 1 in. wall, 10- and 20-ft lengths.
sections.body: 3.2.1 Tendons (pp. 34-35). Tendons are threaded, either with continuous spirally-deformed ribbing (continuous thread bars) or with threads cut into a bare reinforcing bar. Bars must be threaded a minimum of 6 in. on the cut face to attach the bearing plate and nut; where threads are cut into a non-threaded bar, the reduced steel area in the threaded portion must be considered in design. Tendons generally have a nominal tensile strength of 60 ksi (Grade 60) or 75 ksi (Grade 75) and should conform to ASTM A615. Grade 95 and up to Grade 150 tendons may be considered, but high-grade steel is more typical of ground anchors (Sabatini et al. 1999), whose design loads are much greater, and may not be efficient for conventional soil nails. Grade 95 bars may be acceptable as long as their ductility is comparable to lower-grade steels; Grade 150 bars should conform to ASTM A722. Table A.1 (Appendix A) gives solid bar section properties. Solid bar nails commonly use Nos. 8, 9, 10 and 11. Bars smaller than No. 8 (Nos. 6 and 7) are used by some but often avoided, because they may bend excessively during handling and installation and may lead to too close, inefficient nail spacing. Bars No. 14 and larger may be inefficient because their maximum tensile load is limited by geotechnical pullout and facing strength; these limits do not apply in all cases. The maximum manufactured length of threaded bars is 60 ft for No. 6 through No. 14. Tendons are generally continuous without splices or welds; couplers can extend them and must develop the nominal tensile resistance of the bars as certified by the manufacturer (Figure 3.2). Hollow bars range in yield strength between 60 and 90 ksi (410 and 620 MPa), from about 1 to 3 in. (30 to 73 mm) outer diameter and 0.3 to 1 in. (7 to 25 mm) wall thickness, in 10- and 20-ft lengths that can be cut and coupled; Tables A.2 to A.4 give their section properties.
key_points: Threaded bars: continuous thread or cut threads (account for reduced area); at least 6 in. of thread on the cut face
Grade 60 or 75 (60 or 75 ksi) per ASTM A615 generally used
Grade 95 acceptable if ductility comparable to lower grades; Grade 150 per ASTM A722, more typical of ground anchors
Common sizes Nos. 8, 9, 10, 11; Nos. 6-7 often avoided; No. 14 and larger may be inefficient
Maximum manufactured length 60 ft for Nos. 6-14; couplers must develop the bar's nominal tensile resistance
Hollow bars: yield 60-90 ksi, OD about 1-3 in., wall 0.3-1 in., 10- and 20-ft lengths
Section properties: Table A.1 (solid), Tables A.2-A.4 (hollow), Appendix A

sections.title: Connection Components
sections.summary: Bearing plate, beveled washers, hex nuts, washers and headed studs connect the nail to the facing. The plate spreads the nail-end force onto the initial shotcrete and soil: commonly Grade 36 (AASHTO M183/ASTM A36) or Grade 50, square and flat, 8 to 10 in. sides, 0.75 to 1 in. thick; well seated but not excessively embedded in fresh shotcrete. Beveled washers or spherical seat nuts give uniform bearing; nuts hand-wrench tightened, not over-tightened after set; AASHTO M291/ASTM A563 Grade B. Typically four headed studs welded to the plate (ANSI/AWS 2000), commonly 1 to 1.5 in. from the plate edges.
sections.body: 3.2.2 Connection Components (pp. 35-37). The steel components connecting nails to the facing are bearing plates, beveled washers, hexagonal nuts, washers and headed studs (Figure 3.3). The bearing plate, nuts and washers connect the nail to the initial facing; the headed studs connect the nail end to the final facing. The bearing plate distributes the force at the nail end onto the initial shotcrete and the soil behind it. It is commonly Grade 36 (AASHTO M183/ASTM A36) or Grade 50 steel, usually square and flat, with 8- to 10-in. sides and typical thicknesses of 0.75 to 1 in. Some manufacturers supply forged plates concave at the drill hole, allowing some articulation in any direction. Most Contractors place the plate against the still-fresh shotcrete; it must be well-seated but not excessively embedded into the grout. Beveled washers matching the nail inclination are placed between plate and nut for uniform bearing; alternatively, spherical seat nuts facilitate alignment. Nuts are tightened slightly with a hand-wrench, and care must be taken not to over-tighten them after the shotcrete sets. Washers and nuts must meet AASHTO M291/ASTM A563 Grade B. The connection to the final facing typically consists of four headed studs welded to the bearing plate and embedded in the final facing, welded per the Structural Welding Code (ANSI/AWS 2000). The plate should be sized so that studs are no closer to any outer edge than a distance that depends on the stud shaft diameter and is commonly between 1 and 1.5 in.
key_points: Plate, nut and washers connect to the initial facing; headed studs connect to the final facing
Bearing plate: Grade 36 (AASHTO M183/ASTM A36) or Grade 50; square, 8-10 in. sides, 0.75-1 in. thick
Plate well seated in fresh shotcrete but not excessively embedded
Beveled washers or spherical seat nuts for uniform bearing
Nuts hand-wrench tightened; avoid over-tightening after shotcrete sets; AASHTO M291/ASTM A563 Grade B
Typically four headed studs welded to the plate (ANSI/AWS 2000), commonly 1-1.5 in. from plate edges

sections.title: Grout
sections.summary: Most often neat cement grout: minimum 1,500 psi at 3 days and 3,000 to 4,000 psi at 28 days (AASHTO T106/ASTM C109). Cement Types I, II, III, V or I/II (AASHTO M85/ASTM C150); Type I for most uses. Water/cement ratio 0.4 to 0.5 (specific gravity 1.8 to 1.9); specific gravity can be the primary QC if pre-production cube tests prove the mix. Sand/cement grout or ground pre-treatment where grout take must be limited; grout socks in open gravels. No calcium chloride accelerators; air entrainment only with other protection or extra cover. Tremie from the hole bottom; fill the 'bird's beak'.
sections.body: 3.2.3 Grout (pp. 37-39). Grout fills the annulus between tendon and soil and is most often a neat cement grout. Minimum compressive strength should be 1,500 psi at 3 days and 3,000 to 4,000 psi at 28 days (AASHTO T106/ASTM C109); sand, if used, must meet AASHTO M6/ASTM C33 (Figure 3.4, grout plant). Cement Types I, II, III, V or I/II (AASHTO M85/ASTM C150) can be used. Type I (general purpose) is recommended for most applications; Type II (moderate sulfate resistance) hardens more slowly, produces less heat and resists sulfates better; Type III (high early strength) is finer and hardens faster; Type V (high sulfate resistance) may be used where ground is corrosive. The water/cement ratio for neat cement grout ranges from 0.4 to 0.5, equivalent to a specific gravity of 1.8 to 1.9. Specific gravity measured during preparation (Figure 3.5) gives immediate results and can be the primary QC if pre-production compression tests on cubes of known specific gravity show the mix consistently reaches the minimum strength; cubes may still be tested periodically (Figure 3.6). A stiffer, less flowable sand/cement grout may control leakage into highly permeable granular soils or fractured rock, but grout that is too stiff cannot be pumped and makes tendon installation difficult or impossible, so ground pre-treatment may be needed; specific gravity is not suitable QC for sand/cement grout. In open, cohesionless soils (e.g., poorly graded gravel) a grout sock, a geotextile sheath around the bar and tremie pipe, may be needed to prevent hole collapse and reduce grout flow. Admixtures are not typically required; admixtures controlling bleed, flowability, water content, set and workability may be used if they meet AASHTO M194/ASTM C494 and are compatible. Accelerators are generally not permitted; calcium chloride accelerators must be avoided because they drastically increase corrosion potential. Expansive admixtures should not be permitted except in encapsulation grout (Chapter 7). Plasticizers can extend workability up to about one hour (hot climates, long pumping). Air-entrainment improves workability and reduces cracking but opens the matrix and reduces corrosion protection, so it should be approved only with other corrosion protection or grout cover thicker than the Chapter 7 minimums. Shrinkage-limiting proprietary grouts are desirable; test grout and bond where admixtures are considered. With solid bars, grout is pumped shortly after the tendon is placed, by tremie through a pipe inserted to the bottom of the hole, until the hole is full. The inclined hole leaves a void at the mouth (the 'bird's beak'), filled with grout behind a temporary cover or, more commonly, with shotcrete by hand-packing or during facing placement; it is the area most vulnerable to water and corrosion and must be filled. Grout pipes are heavy-duty plastic tubing of approximately 0.75 to 1.0 in. outer diameter, commonly removed; if left in, they should be plugged at the proximal end, or their effect considered. Injection must be smooth and continuous with no voids, the tube bottom kept below the grout surface; often the whole hole is filled before the tube is withdrawn. HBSN grouting: Chapter 10.
key_points: Neat cement grout: minimum 1,500 psi at 3 days, 3,000-4,000 psi at 28 days (AASHTO T106/ASTM C109)
Cement Types I, II, III, V or I/II (AASHTO M85/ASTM C150); Type I recommended for most uses; Type V where corrosive
Water/cement ratio 0.4-0.5 = specific gravity 1.8-1.9; specific gravity as primary QC once the mix is proven by cubes
Sand/cement grout or ground pre-treatment to limit grout take; grout sock in open gravels
Admixtures per AASHTO M194/ASTM C494; no accelerators, never calcium chloride
Air entrainment only with other corrosion protection or extra grout cover
Tremie from the bottom of the hole; tube bottom kept below the grout surface
Fill the 'bird's beak' at the hole mouth (most vulnerable to corrosion)
Grout tubes 0.75-1.0 in. OD; plug if left in place

sections.title: Centralizers
sections.summary: Centralizers of Schedule 20 or 40 PVC or other synthetics not harmful to the tendon (steel centralizers with HBSNs) keep a minimum grout cover. Installed at intervals not exceeding 10 ft and about 1.5 ft from each end of the nail, securely attached, and sized to hold the tendon within 1 in. of the hole center, let the tremie reach the bottom, and let grout flow freely.
sections.body: 3.2.4 Centralizers (p. 41). Centralizers are made of Schedule 20 or 40 polyvinyl chloride (PVC) or other synthetic materials not detrimental to the tendon (Figure 3.8); steel centralizers are used with HBSNs (Figure 3.7). They are installed along each solid bar or HBSN so that a minimum thickness of grout completely covers the tendon, at regular intervals not exceeding 10 ft along the nail and at about 1.5 ft from each end. They must be securely attached and sized to allow: (i) positioning the tendon within 1 in. of the center of the drill hole; (ii) inserting the tremie pipe to the bottom of the hole; and (iii) grout to flow freely up the hole.
key_points: Schedule 20 or 40 PVC or other non-detrimental synthetics; steel centralizers with HBSNs
Spacing not exceeding 10 ft; about 1.5 ft from each end of the nail
Tendon within 1 in. of the drill hole center
Must let the tremie reach the bottom and grout flow freely

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Elements
sections.summary: Besides cement grout: encapsulation of solid bars in corrugated HDPE (AASHTO M252) or PVC (ASTM D1784 Class 13464-B) sheath, grouted at the factory, then tremie grouted in the hole; fusion-bonded epoxy coating (ASTM A775), green (flexible) or gray and purple (more chemical resistance; purple for marine or harsh environments); hot-dip galvanizing; and sacrificial steel, a thickness subtracted from the bar for non-aggressive soils. Coatings on HBSNs are likely damaged during drilling. Selection in Chapter 7.
sections.body: 3.2.5 Corrosion Protection Elements (pp. 42-43). In addition to cement grout, which gives physical and chemical protection, other devices add protection as needed. Solid bars can be encapsulated in a sheath of corrugated high-density polyethylene (HDPE) conforming to AASHTO M252, or corrugated PVC tube conforming to ASTM D1784 Class 13464-B; the annulus between sheath and tendon is grouted before leaving the manufacturer, and the annulus between sheath and drill hole is tremie grouted after placement. Fusion-bonded epoxy coating (ASTM A775) is a dielectric that impedes corrosion currents. Coatings are green, gray or purple: green is flexible and suits bent reinforcement; gray and purple are less flexible but more chemically resistant; purple is better suited for marine or harsh environments (Figure 3.9). Manufacturers have tested abrasion resistance, but there are not sufficient data to correlate abrasion test results with field performance. Solid and hollow tendons and hardware can be hot-dip galvanized, but because HBSNs drill with the bar itself, galvanizing and epoxy coatings are likely damaged during installation (Cadden et al. 2010; Samtani and Nowatzki 2010). The simplest protection is sacrificial steel: for non-aggressive soils, a nominal thickness depending on the design life is subtracted from the bar diameter for structural resistance calculations. Chapter 7 describes protection methods and selection; Chapter 10 covers HBSNs.
key_points: Encapsulation: corrugated HDPE (AASHTO M252) or PVC (ASTM D1784 Class 13464-B) sheath, factory grouted
Fusion-bonded epoxy coating per ASTM A775 (dielectric)
Green epoxy flexible; gray and purple more chemically resistant; purple for marine or harsh environments
No reliable correlation between abrasion test results and field coating performance
Hot-dip galvanizing possible; coatings on HBSNs likely damaged during drilling
Sacrificial steel: thickness by design life subtracted for non-aggressive soils

sections.title: Wall Facing
sections.summary: Initial facing (shotcrete with WWM, waler bars and vertical bars at nail heads) supports soil between nails during construction, connects nails and prevents erosion; final facing (CIP reinforced concrete or WWM-reinforced shotcrete, or precast panels) does the same long term and meets aesthetics, considering corrosion and climate. WWM Grades 60-80 (AASHTO M55/ASTM A1064); rebar AASHTO M31/ASTM A615. Shotcrete, wet or dry process, is mortar or small-aggregate concrete consolidated by impact; strength verified on cored test panels (ASTM C1604); polyethylene film (AASHTO M171) for curing.
sections.body: 3.2.6 Wall Facing (pp. 43-45). Tendons connect to a facing at the excavation face or slope surface, most commonly an initial facing of shotcrete and a final facing of shotcrete or CIP concrete. The initial facing supports the exposed soil between nails during excavation and installation, provides initial connection among nails, and protects against erosion and sloughing; the final facing performs the same functions and allows the project's aesthetic requirements to be met, and its design must consider long-term corrosion and climate variations as needed. Initial facing most commonly consists of shotcrete, WWM, and short waler and vertical bars around the nail heads; final facing is commonly CIP reinforced concrete or WWM-reinforced shotcrete. WWM is manufactured in Grades 60, 65, 70, 75 and 80 (minimum wire yield strength in ksi), plain or deformed (WRI 2006), and must meet AASHTO M55/ASTM A1064 or ASTM 1064M (as printed). Reinforcing steel must meet AASHTO M31/ASTM A615, Grade 420, deformed. Precast panels may form the final facing, especially for special aesthetics. Typical WWM sizes and properties: Table A.5 (Appendix A). Shotcrete, mortar or small-aggregate concrete, is sprayed pneumatically at high velocity onto the soil, and the impact energy consolidates it; it can be applied by a wet or dry process (PCA 2013). Strength and consistency are verified on test panels that are cored and tested for compressive strength per ASTM C1604 (Figures 3.10, 3.11). Polyethylene film meeting AASHTO M171 can control moisture loss after application.
key_points: Initial facing: shotcrete with WWM, waler bars and vertical bars at nail heads
Final facing: CIP reinforced concrete, WWM-reinforced shotcrete, or precast panels
Final facing design considers long-term corrosion and climate
WWM Grades 60-80 (yield in ksi), AASHTO M55/ASTM A1064; properties in Table A.5
Reinforcing steel AASHTO M31/ASTM A615, deformed
Shotcrete: mortar or small-aggregate concrete, wet or dry process (PCA 2013)
Test panels cored and tested per ASTM C1604; curing film per AASHTO M171

sections.title: Drainage
sections.summary: Vertical geocomposite strip drains behind the initial facing limit water pressure: polymer core with minimum compressive strength 40 psi (ASTM D1621 Procedure A) and, with geotextile, minimum flow 0.1 gallons per second per foot of width (ASTM D4716). Strips discharge through PVC caps and exit pipes to an underdrain (Schedule 40 PVC; slotted PVC or PE pipe in clean coarse gravel) and/or weepholes. Wrap the aggregate trench in geotextile meeting filter criteria (Holtz et al. 2008), not the pipe. Abundant groundwater needs horizontal drains and a careful feasibility review.
sections.body: 3.2.7 Drainage (pp. 45-46). To limit water pressure behind the facing, vertical geocomposite strip drains are installed behind the initial facing against the excavation face (Figure 3.12). They consist of a drainage core (polypropylene, polyester, polyamine, PVC, polyolefin or polystyrene) and a filtration geotextile attached to or encapsulating it. The core should have a minimum compressive strength of 40 psi (ASTM D1621 Procedure A), and the core fully encapsulated by geotextile a minimum flow rate of 0.1 gallons per second per foot of strip width (ASTM D4716). Strips are fitted with drainage elements that let water exit to the outside of the wall, discharging into a pipe drain along the base and/or through weepholes through the facing to the toe. Most drainage elements are PVC: a snap-on cap or grate and an exit pipe connected to the underdrain. The underdrain is generally a drainage pipe in an aggregate-filled trench along the bottom of the excavation; pipe and fittings should meet Schedule 40 PVC solid and perforated wall requirements; the pipe is slotted PVC or polyethylene (PE) surrounded by clean coarse gravel free of fines. The aggregate trench must be wrapped with geotextile filter fabric; a geotextile sock directly over the slotted pipe must be avoided. The geotextile prevents piping of fines from the surrounding soil, should meet filter criteria (Holtz et al. 2008), and is selected from the retained soil's gradation; the aggregate collects water along the pipe, a redundant pathway. Where groundwater behind the wall is abundant, horizontal pipe drains into the retained soil are necessary; with large volumes or high groundwater, the applicability of soil nails versus other technologies should be carefully evaluated in the feasibility study. Great care is needed where significant seepage or high groundwater exists. Drainage design: Chapter 6.
key_points: Vertical geocomposite strip drains behind the initial facing
Core minimum compressive strength 40 psi (ASTM D1621 Procedure A)
Minimum flow 0.1 gal/s per foot of strip width (ASTM D4716)
Discharge to an underdrain along the base and/or weepholes to the toe
Underdrain: Schedule 40 PVC fittings; slotted PVC or PE pipe in clean coarse gravel
Wrap the aggregate trench in filter geotextile (Holtz et al. 2008); no geotextile sock on the pipe
Abundant groundwater: horizontal pipe drains; re-evaluate soil nail feasibility

sections.title: Construction Methods
sections.summary: Construction activities in detail: excavation (3.3.2), drilling (3.3.3), nail installation and grouting (3.3.4), drainage placement (3.3.5), initial facing (3.3.6) and final facing (3.3.7).
sections.body: 3.3 Construction Methods (pp. 46-60). Subsections 3.3.1 Introduction to 3.3.7 Final Facing Construction.
sections.applicability: Soil nail wall construction methods; see the subsections.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: The construction sequence from Chapter 2: (1) excavation; (2) drilling of nail holes; (3A) nail installation and grouting, (3B) installation of strip drain; (4) initial shotcrete facing; (5) subsequent levels, repeating Steps 1-4; (6) final facing. The following subsections describe each activity.
sections.body: 3.3.1 Introduction (pp. 46-47). The construction sequence introduced in Chapter 2 includes: 1. Excavation; 2. Drilling of nail holes; 3. A) Nail installation and grouting, B) Installation of strip drain; 4. Construction of initial shotcrete facing; 5. Construction of subsequent levels (repeat Steps 1-4); 6. Construction of final facing. Detailed descriptions follow.
key_points: Steps: excavation; drilling; nail installation and grouting with strip drains; initial facing; repeat; final facing
sections.applicability: Order of construction activities.

sections.title: Excavation
sections.summary: Install surface water controls first. Initial cut often 3 to 5 ft; smooth face; hand excavation for cobbles or boulders. Working bench about 30 ft wide for conventional drills; small track drills need 15 ft and 8 to 10 ft headroom. The lowest safety margins often occur while a lower lift is unsupported; watch for bulging, sloughing and excessive deformation and backfill with a berm if seen; expose only what can be shotcreted in one shift. Options for poor stand-up: stabilizing berms (full or in slots no wider than about the nail spacing), permeation grouting, or vertical grouted bars at 1 to 3 ft.
sections.body: 3.3.2 Excavation (pp. 47-50). Before excavation, surface water controls should be installed along the top of the wall, since inflow harms construction and face stability; collector trenches behind the excavation limits intercept and divert surface water. Excavation uses conventional mass excavation or earth-moving equipment from a platform, with final trimming by backhoe or excavator. The initial cut depth is often 3 to 5 ft. The face should be reasonably smooth to avoid excessive shotcrete; cobbles or boulders may require hand excavation. A level working bench on the order of 30 ft wide is required for conventional drilling equipment; small track drills can work on benches as narrow as 15 ft with headroom as low as 8 to 10 ft. The most critical stability condition often occurs during construction: for lower lifts, the lowest margins of safety may occur while the cut is temporarily unsupported, before nails and shotcrete are placed. Watch for early signs of instability (bulging, sloughing, excessive deformation); if seen, quickly backfill the face with a temporary berm. The exposed length should be limited to what can be stabilized and shotcreted in a single shift (Figure 3.13). Where the face cannot stand for the required time, a continuous berm may be left to support it (Figure 3.14): nails are installed and grouted through the berm, then the berm is excavated and shotcrete applied shortly after. Alternatively the berm is removed in a staggered sequence of alternating slots no wider than approximately the nail horizontal spacing: nails and shotcrete in each slot, then the remaining berm sections. Berms significantly affect cost and schedule; if stand-up time is a major concern, consider alternative top-down methods such as soldier piles and ground anchors. Ground improvement such as permeation grouting has been used to improve stand-up time of unstable granular soils (LaRue 2010). As an alternative to berms, vertical grouted bars at 1 to 3 ft horizontal spacing along the base of the wall can give temporary face stability; the print says the spacing should be smaller for soils more prone to face instability. They should only be installed where loose deposits are encountered; a battered wall can be changed to a stepped wall at such locations. Vertical bars may cost more than berms but help the schedule. Some contractors install vertical grout columns (without a bar) next to the face to limit overbreak, give a neat line and prevent ground loss.
key_points: Install surface water controls and collector trenches before excavating
Initial cut often 3 to 5 ft; smooth face; hand excavation for cobbles and boulders
Working bench ~30 ft wide; small track drills: 15 ft bench, 8-10 ft headroom
Lowest safety margin often while a lower lift is unsupported
Signs of instability (bulging, sloughing, deformation): backfill with a temporary berm at once
Expose only what can be shotcreted in one shift
Stabilizing berm: nails through the berm, or slots no wider than about the nail horizontal spacing
Alternatives: soldier piles and anchors, permeation grouting (LaRue 2010), vertical grouted bars at 1-3 ft

sections.title: Drilling of Nail Holes
sections.summary: Rotary, percussion, auger or rotary-percussion drilling, compatible with ground, nail length and diameter (Table 3.1a-c). Drilling must not cause excessive mining, caving or heave of the upper rows; use casing or HBSNs in unstable ground or limit air flush. The Contractor usually picks the method, though the designer may restrict methods that threaten adjacent structures or utilities. Cased drilling (single tube, duplex rotary) generally gives 7-in. holes and can raise costs significantly.
sections.body: 3.3.3 Drilling of Nail Holes (pp. 50-52). Nail holes are drilled by rotary, percussion, auger or rotary-percussion methods. Table 3.1 (a, b, c) summarizes common equipment and methods; the equipment must suit the ground and the required nail length and diameter (Figure 3.15, external flush open hole). Table 3.1a, hydraulic rotary auger methods for competent soils or weathered rock: lead flight Kelley-bar driven, sectional solid-stem and continuous flight solid-stem (uncased, mechanical cuttings removal); sectional hollow-stem and continuous flight hollow-stem (cased, mechanical with air support); holes 4-12 in. Table 3.1b, hydraulic air and water rotary methods for competent soils, rock or mixed ground (pneumatic down-the-hole hammer available): external flush open hole (uncased, water), external flush cased (cased, water), duplex (cased, compressed air or water); holes 4-8 in. (air rotary) and 4-12 in. (hollow stem augers). Table 3.1c, pneumatic rotary (top hole hammer) for non-caving competent soils or rock: external flush open hole (uncased, compressed air); holes 4-8 in., typically < 5 in. (all after Elias and Juran 1991). Method selection may also depend on local equipment and ground. Drilling should not cause excessive ground mining or caving, and drilling of the upper rows should not cause excessive surface heave; these effects may be avoided with casing or HBSNs in unstable ground, or by limiting the air flush so the hole stays open without building pressure. Contracts commonly let the Contractor choose the method, but the designer may restrict methods or procedures for ground or project reasons, e.g. risk to adjacent structures or utilities. Cased drilling includes the single tube method (cuttings flushed outside the tube by air, water or both) and the duplex rotary method (inner drill rods and outer casing, cuttings removed through the annulus); hole diameters are generally 7 in. Casing increases cost, sometimes significantly.
key_points: Methods: rotary, percussion, auger, rotary-percussion; compatible with ground, nail length and diameter
Table 3.1a auger methods: holes 4-12 in.; hollow-stem methods cased
Table 3.1b air and water rotary: 4-8 in. (air rotary), 4-12 in. (hollow stem augers); duplex cased
Table 3.1c top hole hammer: 4-8 in., typically < 5 in., non-caving ground only
Avoid excessive mining, caving and surface heave: casing, HBSNs or limited air flush
Contractor usually selects the method; designer may restrict it near structures or utilities
Single tube and duplex cased drilling: holes generally 7 in.; casing can raise cost significantly

sections.title: Nail Installation and Grouting
sections.summary: The tendon is inserted and the hole tremie grouted from the bottom. Gravity grouting usually gives enough bond; in granular soils and weak fissured rock, low-pressure grouting through the casing raises bond (confinement, compaction, interlock, larger effective diameter), seldom useful in fine-grained soils. Poor cuttings removal, or over-cleaning that remolds moderately plastic clay, can greatly reduce bond (Chapter 4).
sections.body: 3.3.4 Nail Installation and Grouting (pp. 52-53). After the tendon is inserted (Figure 3.16), the hole is filled with grout through a tremie pipe inserted to the bottom, and the grout bonds to the tendon and ground as it sets. Gravity grouting provides bond strengths often sufficient for soil nailing to be feasible and cost-effective. Where poor soils require higher bond strength to keep nail lengths reasonable, high bond can be achieved in granular soils and weak fissured rock by injecting grout under relatively low pressure through the casing; the increase results from higher confining pressure around the grout, compaction of the surrounding soil, increased soil-grout interlocking and a larger effective grout diameter. Pressure grouting through the casing is seldom used in fine-grained soils, where only minor increases are achieved, especially if saturated. The design bond resistance may not be achieved without appropriate procedures: poor removal of cuttings may significantly reduce bond, and in clayey soils of moderate plasticity excessive mechanical cleaning may remold the clay and reduce bond far below undisturbed values. Design bond strength: Chapter 4.
key_points: Tremie grouting from the bottom of the hole after the tendon is inserted
Gravity grouting usually gives sufficient bond
Low-pressure grouting through casing raises bond in granular soils and weak fissured rock
Pressure grouting seldom used in fine-grained soils (minor gain)
Poor cuttings removal or over-cleaning (remolding clay) can greatly reduce bond

sections.title: Drainage Placement
sections.summary: Strip drains go against the face, geotextile side to the soil; rolls are protected during shotcreting and unrolled; panel drains are spliced at each lift bottom with a minimum 12-in. overlap of core and geotextile. Drain caps and exit pipes are fixed to the facing steel and protected from shotcrete. The underdrain trench at the toe is wrapped in geotextile around clean aggregate and pipe; geotextile-wrapped pipe generally not recommended. Continuity of the drainage path at every joint is key.
sections.body: 3.3.5 Drainage Placement (pp. 53-54). Strip drains are placed against the excavation face with the geotextile filter side against the soil. Rolls must be protected while shotcrete is applied to each lift and then rolled down to be continuous. Panel-type drains must be spliced at the bottom of each lift, generally with a minimum 12-in. overlap of both core and geotextile so flow and filtration are not impeded. The bottom drainage cap and exit pipe are connected to the strips and fixed to the facing reinforcement; the exit pipe must be covered during shotcreting, then connected to the underdrain if applicable. The underdrain is built in a trench at the toe: geotextile is placed in the trench, the clean aggregate and drainage pipes are placed, and the geotextile is wrapped across the top. A geotextile-wrapped pipe is generally not recommended. Continuity of the drainage path is key between drainage core joints, between core and weephole outlets, between wall outlet and drain pipe, and between drain pipe and drain outlet.
key_points: Geotextile filter side against the soil
Panel drains spliced at each lift bottom with a minimum 12-in. overlap of core and geotextile
Protect exit pipes from shotcrete; connect to the underdrain afterward
Underdrain trench wrapped in geotextile; geotextile-wrapped pipe generally not recommended
Keep the drainage path continuous at every joint and outlet

sections.title: Initial Facing Construction
sections.summary: Initial shotcrete most commonly 3 to 4 in. thick, with WWM or fibers and bars, leaving a band at the lift bottom for overlaps. Wet mix often preferred (2.2-3.0 vs 1.5-3.0 yd3/h; rebound about 5% vs 15%); w/c about 0.4, below 0.45 for strength and durability; cement about 600-700 lb/yd3; about 5% strength loss per 1% air. Tolerances 1.5 to 2 times CIP values; taper shift-end joints to about 1 in. WWM width = lift height plus at least one mesh cell (4-8 ft sheets; 12.5-25 ft lengths, up to 40 ft); two walers and two vertical bars at each nail.
sections.body: 3.3.6 Initial Facing Construction (pp. 54-57). 3.3.6a General: the initial facing is shotcrete, most commonly 3 to 4 in. thick, thicker in special applications; it forms a continuous layer and fills irregularities, reinforced with WWM or fibers and bars. It covers the exposed soil except a narrow band at the bottom of the lift, left to expose the lowest WWM and strip drains for overlap with the next lift (Figure 3.17). 3.3.6b Shotcrete Application: shootability (sticking, building thickness, resisting sloughing; high flow resistance and viscosity) and pumpability (flowing like a viscous fluid; low flow resistance and viscosity) are opposing requirements. With a proper mix, shootability up to typically 6 to 8 in. is achieved without sloughing or sag cracks below the rebar; thinner initial facings make it a non-issue (mix design: ACI 2014). Dry mix: aggregate and cement blended dry, water added at the nozzle, accelerators the most common admixture on vertical surfaces. Wet mix: all ingredients batched and pumped to the nozzle, applied by compressed air at higher velocity. Wet mix is often preferred because it yields somewhat higher production (typically 2.2 to 3.0 yd3/hour versus 1.5 to 3.0 for dry mix), rebound is often only about 5 percent versus 15 percent, no water is added at the nozzle (less dependent on the nozzle operator), and ready-mix supply is readily available. Both methods use a water/cement ratio of about 0.4 and give roughly the same quality, wet mix a slightly greater flexural strength; w/c about 0.4 with air entrainment (difficult with dry mix) enhances durability, and w/c below 0.45 tends to give high strength and durability and low permeability if compacted in situ. Cement content (approximately 600 to 700 lb/yd3) and in situ density are key; increasing air reduces strength (5 percent per approximately 1 percent of air). Initial facing durability requirements may be relaxed relative to final facing but are usually similar. Steel fibers in wet mix increase ductility, toughness and impact resistance with only modest flexural gain. CIP tolerances cannot easily be met; initial facing tolerances should be on the order of 1.5 to 2 times those for CIP concrete. Contraction or construction joints are generally not required; vertical joints follow the daily exposed length and horizontal joints approximately the lift height. At the end of a shift, taper the shotcrete from full thickness to an edge up to approximately 1 in., and clean the joint with compressed air and wet it before the next section. 3.3.6c Shotcrete Reinforcement: WWM sheets are the common initial facing reinforcement (occasionally final), sized for flexure, punching shear and constructability (Appendix A). Panel width must equal the lift height (vertical nail spacing) plus at least one full mesh cell; U.S. WWM comes in 4- to 8-ft wide sheets and rolls, sheets in 12.5-, 15-, 20- and 25-ft lengths, up to 40 ft on request, and laps must meet ACI/AASHTO development provisions. For remote sites check local WWM widths; the designer may adjust the vertical nail spacing to suit them. Walers and vertical bars around the nail heads add flexural resistance: generally two horizontal walers and two vertical bars, one on each side of the nail (Figure 3.18).
key_points: Initial shotcrete most commonly 3 to 4 in. thick; band left at the lift bottom for WWM and drain overlap
Shootability typically up to 6-8 in. per pass with a proper mix
Wet mix often preferred: 2.2-3.0 vs 1.5-3.0 yd3/h; rebound ~5% vs ~15%
w/c about 0.4; below 0.45 for high strength, durability and low permeability
Cement ~600-700 lb/yd3; ~5% strength loss per ~1% air
Tolerances ~1.5 to 2 times CIP tolerances
Shift joints tapered to ~1 in., cleaned with air and wetted
WWM width = lift height plus at least one full mesh cell; sheets 4-8 ft wide, 12.5-25 ft long (up to 40 ft)
Two horizontal walers and two vertical bars at each nail head

sections.title: Final Facing Construction
sections.summary: Reinforced shotcrete final facing often 6 to 12 in. beyond the initial facing, built in layers, usually bottom up after the last lift, connected by headed studs; walers usually not needed; vertical contraction joints typically 45 to 90 ft, not over nails. CIP facing: rebar both ways plus short bars at nail heads, form liners, one-sided forms tied to the nails acceptable; joints typically 90 to 100 ft (printed as similar to shotcrete). Precast: 5 ft by 5 ft segmental or full-height tilt-up panels, structural or not; templates ensure accurate nail location.
sections.body: 3.3.7 Final Facing Construction (pp. 58-60). 3.3.7a Reinforced Shotcrete: total thickness often between 6 and 12 in., excluding the initial facing; headed studs welded to the bearing plates connect it to the nails. It is built in successive layers, usually (not always) after the deepest initial facing lift, advancing from the bottom up; it can also be built as excavation progresses, with care to support its weight during later lifts. Reinforcement is WWM or rebar (available WWM may not give an efficient design); waler bars are usually not required. Because nail heads give fixed points approximately every 5 ft, vertical contraction joint requirements can be less restrictive than for other walls; maximum spacing in permanent shotcrete facing is typically 45 to 90 ft, adjusted to avoid placing joints over nails. For aesthetics, wood, steel or rubber tools can smooth and groove the surface, pigmented sealers can color it, and the final shotcrete may be thickened, sculpted and stained to match nearby rock (the print refers to 'Section 3.5' for sculpted faces; the material is Section 3.4.1). 3.3.7b Cast-in-Place Reinforced Concrete: routinely reinforced with vertical and horizontal rebar and short supplementary bars around the nail head; commercial form liners give various finishes (Figure 3.19); one-sided formwork tied to the nails is generally acceptable if facing performance and nail corrosion protection are not compromised. Advantages over shotcrete: form liners, uniform appearance, homogeneous quality. Maximum vertical contraction joint spacing in permanent CIP facing is typically 90 to 100 ft, which the print calls similar to shotcrete final facings (given above as 45 to 90 ft). 3.3.7c Precast Concrete Facing: used in permanent walls for aesthetics and durability (Figure 3.20); allows a continuous drainage blanket and/or a frost protection barrier behind the facing. Panels are small segmental (5 ft by 5 ft) or full-height tilt-up elements, structural (carrying the nail head load, via stud connectors or hoop-shaped rebar at the panel back, with low-strength concrete filling the gap; some details patented) or non-structural, in which case the initial facing must be strengthened for the design loads. Connections include truncated wedging heads at panel corners at each nail; nail templates are used because connections need precise nail location. Special nonstructural precast panels, masonry stone or blocks may be placed in front of a shotcrete or CIP final facing for architectural requirements.
key_points: Reinforced shotcrete final facing often 6-12 in. beyond the initial facing; layers, usually bottom up
Headed studs connect the final facing; walers usually not needed in shotcrete final facing
Shotcrete vertical contraction joints typically 45-90 ft, not over nails
CIP: rebar both ways plus short bars at nail heads; form liners; one-sided forms tied to nails acceptable
CIP vertical contraction joints typically 90-100 ft (printed as similar to shotcrete)
Precast: 5 ft x 5 ft segmental or full-height tilt-up; structural or non-structural
Non-structural precast: strengthen the initial facing for the design loads
Templates for nail installation where connections need precise nail location

sections.title: Sculpted Wall Facing
sections.summary: Sculpted facing is a CIP concrete wall hand-sculpted to resemble stone or brick and often stained to match the surroundings; it adds construction cost but gives Owners more aesthetic options.
sections.body: 3.4.1 Sculpted Wall Facing (pp. 60-61). As an alternative to traditional final facings, sculpted wall facing gives a highly aesthetic product: a CIP concrete wall hand-sculpted to resemble stone or brick and often stained to match the surrounding environment. It adds construction cost but offers Owners additional aesthetic options (Figures 3.21, 3.22).
key_points: CIP concrete hand-sculpted to resemble stone or brick, often stained
Adds cost; offers more aesthetic options

sections.title: Drilled Drainage with Hollow Bar Soil Nails
sections.summary: A highly permeable cement-aggregate filter grout can make an HBSN act as a drilled (sub)horizontal drain, relieving water pressure more efficiently than weepholes. Drains must intercept seepage well before it reaches the wall and help reduce pore pressures and ice pressure at the facing; typically installed in one operation without casing by rotary percussion drilling. If deep drains are needed, re-evaluate whether a soil nail wall is appropriate.
sections.body: 3.4.2 Drilled Drainage with Hollow Bar Soil Nails (p. 62). A grout designed to act as a filter (a highly permeable mix of cement and aggregate) can be installed as part of an HBSN, letting it also act as a drilled (sub)horizontal drain that relieves hydrostatic pressure and drains more efficiently than weepholes at the front of the wall. However, if deep drains behind the face need to be considered, a soil nail wall should be carefully evaluated, as it may not be the most appropriate alternative for permanent earth retention. Drilled drains must intercept groundwater seepage well before it approaches the wall; they also help reduce pore water pressures and avoid ice pressure near the facing during freezing. They are typically installed in a single operation, without casing, by rotary percussion drilling.
key_points: Filter grout (permeable cement and aggregate) lets an HBSN act as a drilled drain
More efficient than weepholes; reduces pore pressure and ice pressure at the facing
Must intercept seepage well before it reaches the wall
Single operation, no casing, rotary percussion drilling
Need for deep drains: re-evaluate whether a soil nail wall is appropriate
